# Ephe engine advisory register — flaws that reach us through a native engine
#
# This file exists because the Python register cannot see this class of flaw at all.
# `pip-audit` asks the PyPI ecosystem about the *pip package*; the cell's execution
# engine is Rust, shipped inside the `wasmtime` wheel as a compiled library, and its
# advisories live in the crates.io/RustSec ecosystem. Measured 2026-10-09:
# `POST https://api.osv.dev/v1/query` for `{package: wasmtime, ecosystem: PyPI,
# version: 47.0.1}` returns **zero** vulnerabilities, while the same engine version in
# the `wasmtime-wasi` crate range is under an active advisory. So an entry here is
# never a `--ignore-vuln` flag — pip-audit would not have reported it — it is the
# written acceptance of a flaw our own audit cannot see, and
# `.github/workflows/supply-chain.yml` resolves every ID in this file and in
# `advisories-ignore.txt` against the advisory databases, failing the run on an ID
# that resolves nowhere (that is how `GHSA-j2g9-4prp-pf6h` was nearly lost: a
# well-formed ID that only exists as an *alias*, which the naive lookup reads as a 404).
#
# Line format: <ID>  # package=<name> ecosystem=<eco> probe=<version>
#                    affected=<range> fixed_in=<version> blocked_by=<constraint>
#                    alias=<the GHSA string for the same record, if any> recheck=<YYYY-MM-DD>
# The alias is written down because it is the form a reader searches for and the
# form a single-route lookup reports as missing.
# `probe` is the version the resolution check asks the databases about, and
# `blocked_by` names the constraint that keeps the fix out of reach — an acceptance
# without it would be a shrug. Past its recheck date the gate fails, same rule as the
# other register: the decision carries the date it stops being valid.

# GHSA-j2g9-4prp-pf6h = RUSTSEC-2026-0314 (the RustSec entry is the primary record;
# the GHSA string is an alias of it, and the canonical advisory sits in the
# bytecodealliance/wasmtime repository, not in the pip ecosystem).
# Why there is no fix within reach: affected `wasmtime-wasi` 37.0.0 through 48.0.2,
# fixed in 48.0.3, but every published Ephemora Cell release — 1.0.4.3, 1.0.5 and
# 1.1.0 alike — requires `wasmtime<48,>=43.0.1` in its own METADATA, and `uv.lock`
# resolves wasmtime 47.0.1. The bundled library in the installed wheel
# (wasmtime/darwin-aarch64/_libwasmtime.dylib) carries a 47.x version token. So no
# upgrade of the cell, and no upgrade of the binding, reaches 48.0.3 while the cell
# holds its ceiling: moving past it is Ephemora's release decision, not ours.
# Exposure as measured: CVSS 3.1 AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H — a guest that
# hands the host a datetime beyond its range panics the host process, on the
# in-process path. Ephe does not use that path: `core/cpython_cell.py:200` calls
# `ephemora_cell.run_isolated()`, which in the installed runtime dispatches
# exclusively to `process_executor.run_isolated` → `process_worker`, i.e. a
# disposable worker subprocess, and a guest panic costs that worker. UNPROVEN: that
# the subprocess boundary contains every variant of the flaw (the overflow itself,
# and any state the worker shares before it dies), and whether the 47.x engine in the
# Linux wheel we ship on x86_64 carries the same code path — measured here on
# darwin-arm64 only.
RUSTSEC-2026-0314  # package=wasmtime-wasi ecosystem=crates.io probe=47.0.1 affected=>=37.0.0,<48.0.3 fixed_in=48.0.3 blocked_by=ephemora-cell-requires-wasmtime<48 alias=GHSA-j2g9-4prp-pf6h recheck=2027-01-09

# Re-check protocol for the entries above:
#   1. Ask the engine, not the changelog: which `wasmtime` does the installed
#      `ephemora-cell` require (`*.dist-info/METADATA`, `Requires-Dist`), and which
#      engine version does the binding's library carry?
#   2. Re-read the advisory at its primary record (`https://api.osv.dev/v1/vulns/<id>`)
#      and confirm the affected range still covers the version we resolve.
#   3. Re-check the mitigation claim against the code, not against this file: the
#      panic-containment argument holds only while `core/cpython_cell.py` goes through
#      `run_isolated`/`process_executor`. If an in-process call appears, this entry
#      stops being an acceptance and becomes a defect.
#   4. If Ephemora Cell lifts its wasmtime ceiling past 48.0.3, this line leaves the
#      register with the version that proves it — deleting a line without a
#      replacement version is not a fix.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The rest of the same wave. Asked OSV for exactly what we lock
# (`wasmtime-wasi@47.0.1`, crates.io) answers five advisories; the entry above is the
# one `docs/SANDBOX_EXECUTION.md` had noticed. All four below
# are fixed in 48.0.4, which is out of reach for the same reason: every published
# Ephemora Cell release requires `wasmtime<48`.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Fuel accounting is the cap `core/cpython_cell.py` sets first (DEFAULT_MAX_FUEL,
# 20 G ≈ 2.2 s of guest CPU) and `core/cell_policy.policy_snapshot()` reports it as
# enforced. This advisory says a guest reaching `poll_oneoff` on the WASI preview-0
# path is not metered while it waits — so the number on the card overstates the bound
# for exactly that shape of program. Exposure as measured: Ephe's guest is the CPython
# WASI build, and any code it runs may call `time.sleep`/`selectors`, which lower to
# `poll_oneoff`; the remaining bounds are `timeout_seconds` (30 s) and the worker's
# `io_cpu_seconds` wall, which the subprocess path does enforce. UNPROVEN: whether a
# waiting guest can hold a session past `timeout_seconds`, and how much host wall the
# unmetered wait actually costs — never measured against this engine build.
RUSTSEC-2026-0321  # package=wasmtime-wasi ecosystem=crates.io probe=47.0.1 affected=>=37.0.0,<48.0.4 fixed_in=48.0.4 blocked_by=ephemora-cell-requires-wasmtime<48 alias=GHSA-j366-h8gg-77pm recheck=2027-01-09

# A guest without stdio makes the host allocate unboundedly.
# Why there is no fix within reach: fixed in 48.0.4, behind the same `wasmtime<48`
# ceiling as the entries above.
# Exposure as measured: the flaw's precondition is a guest started without stdio, and
# Ephe always hands the cell a stdout and a stderr journal (`core/cell_output.py`,
# written into the report by `core/cpython_cell.py`), so we do not run that shape.
# UNPROVEN: that no code path can start a cell with stdio closed — `run_isolated` is
# the only caller in this tree and it was read, not fuzzed.
RUSTSEC-2026-0322  # package=wasmtime-wasi ecosystem=crates.io probe=47.0.1 affected=>=37.0.0,<48.0.4 fixed_in=48.0.4 blocked_by=ephemora-cell-requires-wasmtime<48 alias=GHSA-gqmc-89g8-p25r recheck=2027-01-09

# `fd_readdir` copies uninitialised struct padding into guest memory: a guest that
# reads a directory can see host bytes it was not given. That is a leak *into* the
# sandbox, which is the one direction our threat model treats as uninteresting for
# trusted guests and interesting for untrusted ones — and Ephe's whole cell premise is
# untrusted, model-authored code (`docs/SECURITY_THREAT_MODEL.md` §7). Exposure as
# measured: the cell preopens its own session `/work` and the guest root read-only, so
# the readable directories are the ones Ephe put there; the padding bytes would come
# from the host process, not from another session. UNPROVEN: whether anything
# secret-bearing can sit in those bytes in practice, and whether a guest can force a
# readdir on a directory outside the preopens.
RUSTSEC-2026-0323  # package=wasmtime-wasi ecosystem=crates.io probe=47.0.1 affected=>=37.0.0,<48.0.4 fixed_in=48.0.4 blocked_by=ephemora-cell-requires-wasmtime<48 alias=GHSA-96f6-r43r-8c24 recheck=2027-01-09

# The same host-panic timestamp flaw as the first entry, on the wasip3 path and before
# the epoch.
# Why there is no fix within reach: fixed in 48.0.4, and the affected range starts at
# 48.0.0, so it is the one entry here the `<48` ceiling actually keeps out — a fact
# worth stating, because it is the only reason this line is not a live exposure.
# Exposure as measured: Ephe runs the guest on WASI preview 1 through `run_isolated`
# (`core/cpython_cell.py`), which is not the wasip3 path this advisory describes.
# UNPROVEN: that no component guest ever reaches wasip3 — the Python-WASI guest we
# build is preview 1 today, and that is a reading of our build recipe, not a test.
RUSTSEC-2026-0324  # package=wasmtime-wasi ecosystem=crates.io probe=47.0.1 affected=>=48.0.0,<48.0.4 fixed_in=48.0.4 blocked_by=not-on-the-wasip3-path alias=GHSA-mr2v-56j5-cmfc recheck=2027-01-09
